meta.title: Water Challenge, game dataset
meta.basis: Global averages unless stated otherwise. Total water footprint = green + blue + grey. Home use is compared against Irish figures (Uisce Éireann) first, then European ones.
meta.units_note: impact_unit is one of 'L/kg', 'L/L', 'L per unit'. When 'L per unit', unit_detail states exactly what the unit is. Never compare an L/kg row directly with an L per unit row without converting.
meta.research_caveat: In this environment direct page fetching (WebFetch/curl) was blocked for every domain, including waterfootprint.org, hess.copernicus.org and usgs.gov. All verification was done through web search result summaries, not by opening the primary PDFs. Confidence ratings reflect that: 'high' = the exact figure was returned verbatim in search results and matches the canonical Water Footprint Network value; 'medium' = corroborated approximately or by a single source, or sources disagree; 'low' = not confirmed online, relying on recall.

primary_sources.citation: Mekonnen & Hoekstra 2010/2011, 'The green, blue and grey water footprint of crops and derived crop products', Value of Water Research Report No. 47, UNESCO-IHE; peer-reviewed as Hydrol. Earth Syst. Sci. 15: 1577-1600

Mekonnen & Hoekstra 2010/2012, 'The green, blue and grey water footprint of farm animals and animal products', Value of Water Research Report No. 48, UNESCO-IHE; peer-reviewed as Ecosystems 15: 401-415

meta.derived_from: water-data.json v1.0, compiled 2026-08-06, 69 rows, all of them carried over here

pools.per-kg: Foods and goods sold by weight. Every card reads per kg.
pools.per-unit: One of the thing: one egg, one cup, one shower, one flush, one wash cycle, one pair of jeans.
pools.per-litre: Drinks priced by volume. Reference only, not played, see excluded_reason on each row.

meta.units_rule: A round only ever pairs two items that share the same basis and the same pool. Per-kg is never compared with per-unit, and never with per-litre. Every card states its unit on screen.
meta.near_tie_rule: If two items are within 10% of each other the pairing is dropped and another is drawn, because a near-tie is not a fair question.
meta.field_note: Field names follow cards.csv (the Carbon Challenge dataset): title, sub, category, emoji, impact, comment. `impact` is litres of fresh water. Unlike carbon, water figures come on three different bases, so every card also carries `basis` and `pool` and the game only ever pairs two cards from the same pool. `in_play: false` marks reference-only rows.
meta.voice: Every title, desc, comment or intro here is read by a player and is written as Envie speaking. See CLAUDE.md and _DESIGNS/envie-voice-and-text-rewrite-guide.md: plain short sentences, no em-dashes, European spelling, no emoji, facts and sources untouched.
meta.dilemmas_note: Each dilemma names a 'known' card (shown) and a 'guess' card (hidden) by title, and the basis they share. One opens the per-unit half of every run.
meta.origin_note: origin: IE = Irish figure (Uisce Éireann), EU = European figure (EU bodies or UK sources, shown as 'Europe'). Cards without origin are global averages (Water Footprint Network, WHO).

explainer.title: Green, blue and grey water
explainer.intro: I learned a water footprint is really three different things added together. They are not interchangeable.
explainer.green: Green water is the rain a plant drinks straight out of the soil. It is free, it is local, and it is usually the biggest part of a food's footprint.
explainer.blue: Blue water is what we pump or divert from rivers, lakes and groundwater to irrigate crops or run factories. This is the part that can actually drain a river, and it's the one that worries me most.
explainer.grey: Grey water is not water used, it is water dirtied: the amount of clean water it would take to dilute the fertiliser and other pollution from making something, back to a safe level.

cards.title: Beef
cards.comment: Only about 1% is water the cow actually drinks. Almost all of it grows the feed. That reframed beef for me.

cards.title: Lamb (sheep meat)
cards.comment: Sheep drink far less than cattle, yet lamb still comes in second thirstiest of the common meats. Wasn't the order I'd have guessed.

cards.title: Pork
cards.comment: Pigs convert feed to meat faster than cattle, and that cuts pork's water bill by about 60%. Efficiency you can taste, apparently.

cards.title: Chicken
cards.comment: Chicken is the thriftiest common meat, roughly a quarter of beef's water per kilogram. Good news if you like it grilled.

cards.title: Eggs
cards.comment: A kilo of eggs costs less water than a kilo of chicken meat, from that very same bird. Handy to know.

cards.title: One egg
cards.comment: One egg hides about 196 litres, more than a bath and a half. Didn't see that coming from something so small.
cards.source: Derived from Mekonnen & Hoekstra 2012 (3,265 L/kg x 0.06 kg)
cards.unit_detail: per one 60 g egg

cards.title: Butter
cards.comment: It takes roughly 18 litres of milk to make one kilo of butter, which explains the high figure.

cards.title: Cheese
cards.comment: Cheese concentrates milk about tenfold, so a kilo needs about five times the water of a kilo of milk.
cards.note: Corrected 27 Sep 2026 from 3,178 L/kg. Report 48 Table 4 gives 4,264 green + 439 blue + 357 grey = 5,060, and the WFN Product Gallery says 5,060 L/kg (about 95 g of cheese per kg of milk, half the milk's water allocated to the cheese). The 3,178 figure could not be traced to a primary table. The gallery's headline figure for cheese is 3,178, but its own text works through to 5,060, which matches the primary table.
cards.source: Mekonnen & Hoekstra 2012, WFN Report 48, Table 4; WFN Product Gallery

cards.title: Milk
cards.excluded_reason: Sold by volume, so it sits on a per-litre basis and cannot share a round with per-kg or per-unit items. Only four items share that basis, too few for a fair pool, so the per-litre rows are reference only. The 250 ml glass of milk carries the same figure into play.
cards.comment: Every litre of milk in the fridge represents about a thousand litres out in the fields. Small carton, big story.

cards.title: Glass of milk
cards.comment: A single glass of milk carries more hidden water than three full baths. I looked twice at that one.
cards.source: Derived from Mekonnen & Hoekstra 2012 (1,020 L/L x 0.25 L)
cards.unit_detail: per 250 ml glass

cards.title: Chocolate
cards.comment: Kilo for kilo, chocolate is thirstier than beef. Cocoa trees are the reason, and I wasn't ready for that.
cards.source: Water Footprint Network Product Gallery (from Mekonnen & Hoekstra 2011)

cards.title: Cocoa beans
cards.comment: Cocoa has the largest water footprint of any major crop measured by the Water Footprint Network. Top of a list I wasn't expecting.

cards.title: Coffee (roasted beans)
cards.comment: Roasting drives the number up: green beans sit at 15,897 L/kg, roasted ones climb to nearly 19,000. All that from one bean.
cards.source: Mekonnen & Hoekstra 2011, WFN Report 47 (18,925 L/kg roasted; 15,897 L/kg green)

cards.title: Coffee (one cup)
cards.comment: One small cup of coffee took about 132 litres to reach you, roughly 1,000 times its own volume. My cup felt heavier after that.
cards.unit_detail: per 125 ml cup (about 7 g of roasted coffee)

cards.title: Tea (dried leaves)
cards.comment: Tea leaves need less than half the water of coffee beans, and you use fewer grams per cup too. Tea's quietly winning this one.

cards.title: Tea (one cup)
cards.comment: Swapping a coffee for a tea saves about 105 litres, roughly a bath and a bit. Small swap, decent saving.
cards.unit_detail: per 250 ml cup (about 3 g of dried tea)

cards.title: Rice (milled, white)
cards.comment: Rice is the single biggest user of irrigation water on Earth, ahead of wheat and cotton. A grain topping that list took me by surprise.
cards.source: Mekonnen & Hoekstra 2011, WFN Report 47 (paddy rice 1,673 L/kg)

cards.title: Wheat
cards.comment: About 70% of wheat's water is rain the plant drinks straight from the soil, not irrigation. Mostly the sky's doing, not a pump's.

cards.title: Bread
cards.comment: A standard 800 g loaf carries around 1,290 litres, mostly rain that fell on a wheat field long before it was bread.
cards.source: Mekonnen & Hoekstra 2011, WFN Report 47 (derived wheat products)

cards.title: Maize (corn)
cards.comment: Maize is the most efficient major cereal per kilogram, beating both wheat and rice. Fair play to the humble cob.

cards.title: Potatoes
cards.comment: Potatoes are about 80% water themselves, and one of the thriftiest staples you can grow. Good spud, honestly.

cards.title: Pasta (dry)
cards.comment: Dry pasta costs slightly more water than the wheat it came from. Drying it off loses mass, which nudges the number up.
cards.source: Mekonnen & Hoekstra 2011, WFN Report 47 (derived crop products)

cards.title: Soybeans
cards.comment: Most soy never reaches a plate at all. It is grown to feed livestock, not people. That one stuck with me.

cards.title: Tofu
cards.comment: Tofu needs roughly a sixth of beef's water for the same weight of protein-rich food. Worth remembering next time I'm shopping.
cards.source: Water Footprint Network Product Gallery (from Mekonnen & Hoekstra 2011)

cards.title: Lentils
cards.comment: Lentils look thirsty per kilogram, but they are sold dry. Cooked, they roughly triple in weight, so the real number per plate is far lower.

cards.title: Almonds (shelled)
cards.comment: Shelling doubles the figure: half an almond's harvested weight is shell you throw straight away. That's a lot of waste for a snack.
cards.source: Mekonnen & Hoekstra 2011, WFN Report 47 (in-shell about 8,050 L/kg)

cards.title: Walnuts (shelled)
cards.comment: Walnuts come in at roughly half of almonds. Nuts vary a lot more than I expected.
cards.source: Mekonnen & Hoekstra 2011, WFN Report 47 (in-shell about 4,920 L/kg)

cards.title: Peanuts (groundnuts, in shell)
cards.comment: Peanuts are legumes, not nuts, and they drink about a sixth of what almonds do. Good value, all round.

cards.title: Apples
cards.comment: Apple trees are perennial, so their water use is spread over decades of harvests. Patient plants, patient number.

cards.title: One apple
cards.comment: One apple comes to about 125 litres, roughly one and a half baths for a piece of fruit you can eat in five minutes.
cards.source: Derived from Mekonnen & Hoekstra 2011 (822 L/kg x 0.15 kg)
cards.unit_detail: per one 150 g apple

cards.title: Bananas
cards.comment: Bananas grow in the wet tropics, so almost all their water is rain rather than irrigation. The sky does the heavy lifting there.

cards.title: Oranges
cards.comment: Eating the orange beats drinking it: juice needs several fruits squeezed into one glass. Whole fruit wins again.

cards.title: Orange juice
cards.excluded_reason: Sold by volume, so it sits on a per-litre basis and cannot share a round with per-kg or per-unit items. Only four items share that basis, too few for a fair pool, so the per-litre rows are reference only.
cards.comment: A 200 ml glass of orange juice hides about 200 litres. Juicing really concentrates the footprint.
cards.source: Hoekstra 2008, 'The water footprint of food', WFN

cards.title: Tomatoes
cards.comment: Tomatoes are one of the lightest footprint foods there is, about a bath and a half per kilo. Nice one, tomatoes.

cards.title: Lettuce
cards.comment: A whole kilo of lettuce costs less water than a single egg. That one still surprises me.
cards.note: Older Chapagain & Hoekstra (2004) compilations list lettuce at about 130 L/kg.

cards.title: Cabbage
cards.comment: Cabbage stores well for months, so almost none of its water goes to waste through spoilage. Practical vegetable, that.
cards.note: Older WFN compilations list cabbage at about 200 L/kg.

cards.title: Cucumber
cards.comment: A cucumber is about 96% water itself, yet takes only around 350 litres per kilo to grow. Mostly water growing more water.

cards.title: Avocado
cards.comment: One 200 g avocado runs to about 400 litres, nearly ten times a tomato of the same weight. That changed how I see brunch.

cards.title: Olives
cards.comment: Olive trees survive on very little rain, but it takes about five kilos of olives to press one litre of oil. The tree is thrifty, the oil is not.

cards.title: Olive oil
cards.comment: Olive oil is the thirstiest common cooking oil, roughly triple palm oil per kilogram. My favourite topped a chart I wasn't hoping for.

cards.title: Palm oil
cards.comment: Oil palms yield more oil per hectare than any other crop, which keeps their water figure surprisingly low.

cards.title: Sugar cane
cards.comment: Raw cane looks cheap in water terms, but only about a tenth of it ends up as sugar. The rest is stalk and juice lost along the way.

cards.title: Sugar beet
cards.comment: Beet grows in cool, rainy places, so it needs about a third less water than cane. Location does a lot of the work.

cards.title: Refined sugar (from cane)
cards.comment: A single teaspoon of sugar carries roughly seven litres of hidden water. Never looked at my tea the same way since.
cards.source: Mekonnen & Hoekstra 2011, WFN Report 47 (derived crop products)

cards.title: Beer
cards.excluded_reason: Sold by volume, so it sits on a per-litre basis and cannot share a round with per-kg or per-unit items. Only four items share that basis, too few for a fair pool, so the per-litre rows are reference only. The 250 ml glass of beer carries the same figure into play.
cards.comment: Over 90% of beer's footprint is the barley field, not the brewery. The pint is the easy part.
cards.source: Water Footprint Network (from Mekonnen & Hoekstra 2011, barley products)

cards.title: Beer (one glass)
cards.comment: One glass of beer equals about 300 glasses of water once you count the barley behind it. Puts a pint in perspective.
cards.source: Derived from WFN beer figure (298 L/L x 0.25 L)
cards.unit_detail: per 250 ml glass

cards.title: Wine
cards.excluded_reason: Sold by volume, so it sits on a per-litre basis and cannot share a round with per-kg or per-unit items. Only four items share that basis, too few for a fair pool, so the per-litre rows are reference only. The 125 ml glass of wine carries the same figure into play.
cards.comment: Wine costs roughly three times beer per litre, because grapes give less juice per plant. Grapes work harder for less.
cards.source: Mekonnen & Hoekstra 2011, WFN Report 47 (wine grapes 869 m3/tonne)

cards.title: Wine (one glass)
cards.comment: A small glass of wine hides more water than a full bath. That one made me pause mid sip.
cards.note: Older Chapagain & Hoekstra (2004) figures put a 125 ml glass at about 120 litres.
cards.source: Derived from WFN wine figure (869 L/L x 0.125 L)
cards.unit_detail: per 125 ml glass

cards.title: Cotton (lint)
cards.comment: Cotton is the thirstiest non-food crop, and it grows mostly in countries that are already dry. That combination worries me a bit.
cards.note: Seed cotton (unginned) is roughly 3,600 L/kg; the 10,000 figure is for processed lint/fabric.
cards.source: Chapagain, Hoekstra et al. 2006, WFN Report 18 (cotton consumption)

cards.title: Cotton t-shirt
cards.comment: One t-shirt is about 2,500 litres, roughly what one person drinks in three years. I'll think of that next time I'm shopping.
cards.source: Water Footprint Network / Chapagain et al. 2006
cards.unit_detail: per one 250 g cotton t-shirt

cards.title: Pair of jeans
cards.comment: Jeans cost about 8,000 litres, and most of it fell as rain on a cotton field long before the denim did.
cards.source: Water Footprint Network / Chapagain et al. 2006
cards.unit_detail: per one 800 g pair of cotton jeans

cards.title: Pair of leather shoes
cards.comment: Leather shoes inherit the cow's whole footprint. The tanning itself is only a tiny share of the number.
cards.note: Estimates vary widely: 8,000 L/pair is the commonly cited WFN figure, some sources quote 14,000-16,600 L/pair depending on leather weight allocated.
cards.source: Water Footprint Network (bovine leather about 17,100 L/kg)
cards.unit_detail: per one pair of bovine-leather shoes

cards.title: Sheet of A4 paper
cards.comment: Most of a sheet's water is not the mill at all. It is rain the tree drank years before it became paper.
cards.source: Van Oel & Hoekstra 2010, WFN Report 46 (300-2,600 m3/tonne, about 2-13 L per A4 sheet)
cards.unit_detail: per one A4 sheet of 80 gsm printing paper

cards.title: Smartphone
cards.comment: Chip fabs rinse silicon wafers in ultra-pure water hundreds of times per device. Never thought of a phone as thirsty before.
cards.source: Friends of the Earth 'Mind Your Step' report; commonly quoted 12,000-13,000 L
cards.unit_detail: per one smartphone, whole manufacturing chain

cards.title: Car
cards.comment: Over 95% of a car's water is spent before you ever turn the key. All of it gone before the first drive.
cards.note: Older popular figures of 400,000 L per car come from different, broader virtual-water accounting and are not supported by the peer-reviewed LCA.
cards.source: Berger et al. 2012, Environ. Sci. Technol., 'Water Footprint of European Cars'
cards.unit_detail: per one mid-size car, production phase (range 52,000-83,000 L)

cards.title: Shower (per minute)
cards.excluded_reason: A flow rate rather than a single act, and the 7-minute shower row already represents showering in the per-unit pool. Kept here because the reality checks and the actions list both use the 7 litres a minute figure.
cards.comment: A power shower can hit 15 litres a minute, nearly double a standard head. Worth knowing before you crank it up.
cards.source: Uisce Éireann water conservation tips (the average shower uses 7 L a minute)
cards.unit_detail: per minute, average Irish shower
cards.note: Waterwise UK puts a standard UK showerhead at 8 to 10 L a minute (9 L used before 27 Sep 2026). A power shower can reach 15 L a minute.

cards.title: Shower (typical, 7 minutes)
cards.comment: Showers are the single biggest water use in a typical home, about a quarter of the total. Mine included, probably.
cards.source: Uisce Éireann water conservation tips (an average shower uses 49 L in seven minutes)
cards.unit_detail: per one 7-minute shower at 7 L a minute
cards.note: Replaced the UK-derived 8-minute shower at 9 L a minute (72 L) on 27 Sep 2026. The 'quarter of home use' share in the comment is from the Energy Saving Trust, At Home with Water.

cards.title: Bath
cards.comment: A bath and a long shower are surprisingly close. Whichever one runs longer loses, simple as that.
cards.source: Uisce Éireann water conservation page (a typical bath uses 80 litres); Waterwise UK gives the same
cards.unit_detail: per one full bath

cards.title: Toilet flush (old single-flush)
cards.comment: Old cisterns sent up to 13 litres of drinking quality water down the drain with every flush. Straight down for nothing.
cards.source: European Commission water efficiency study; USGS Water Science School
cards.unit_detail: per flush, pre-1990s cistern

cards.title: Toilet flush (modern dual-flush, full)
cards.comment: Dual flush cisterns cut each flush by more than half, and most people never even notice.
cards.source: European Commission water efficiency standards study
cards.unit_detail: per full flush

cards.title: Toilet flush (modern dual-flush, half)
cards.comment: The small button uses 3 litres, about one glass of milk's worth of real water. A tiny button doing real work.
cards.source: European Commission water efficiency standards study
cards.unit_detail: per half flush

cards.title: Dishwasher cycle
cards.comment: A full dishwasher uses about 20 litres. Washing the same load by hand usually takes far more.
cards.source: Uisce Éireann water conservation tips (a dishwasher uses 20 litres)
cards.unit_detail: per cycle, typical machine (Uisce Éireann)
cards.note: Was 10 L (APPLiA Europe, modern machine on eco) until 27 Sep 2026. Switched to the Irish figure; an eco programme on a new machine can use about half.

cards.title: Washing machine cycle
cards.comment: Uisce Éireann puts a washing machine at about 65 litres a cycle. Waiting for a full load is the easy win.
cards.source: Uisce Éireann water conservation tips (a modern washing machine uses about 65 litres a cycle)
cards.unit_detail: per cycle (Uisce Éireann)
cards.note: Was 50 L (APPLiA Europe, about 46 L a cycle in 2022) until 27 Sep 2026. Switched to the Irish figure.

cards.title: Brushing teeth with the tap running
cards.sub: brushing your teeth with the tap running
cards.comment: Two minutes of running tap is 12 litres, twice what a modern toilet flush uses. I'm guilty of that one.
cards.source: Uisce Éireann (a running tap uses up to 6 litres a minute), for a 2-minute brush; Waterwise UK gives the same
cards.unit_detail: per 2-minute brushing at 6 L/min

cards.title: Brushing teeth with the tap off
cards.sub: brushing your teeth with the tap off
cards.comment: Turning the tap off while brushing cuts that step by more than 90%. Small habit, big drop.
cards.source: Uisce Éireann (brushing with the tap off uses about 1 litre); Waterwise UK gives the same
cards.unit_detail: per brushing, wetting brush plus a glass to rinse

cards.title: Dripping tap (per day)
cards.sub: one dripping tap for a day
cards.comment: Uisce Éireann says one dripping tap can waste 5,000 to 10,000 litres a year. For a drip. I checked twice.
cards.source: Uisce Éireann: fixing a dripping tap saves about 150 L a week; one dripping tap wastes 5,000 to 10,000 L a year
cards.unit_detail: per day, one dripping tap (150 L a week / 7; 5,000 to 10,000 L a year is 14 to 27 L a day)
cards.note: Was 15 L a day from the USGS drip calculator and UK utility guidance, replaced with the Irish figure on 27 Sep 2026.

cards.title: Household water use per person per day (Europe)
cards.sub: one day of home water use in Europe
cards.comment: Europeans use about 124 litres a day at home, less than one cup of coffee's hidden water. Puts my own day in perspective.
cards.source: European Environment Agency / Eurostat-based estimates (range about 120-145 L)
cards.unit_detail: per person per day, direct domestic use

cards.title: Household water use per person per day (Ireland)
cards.sub: one day of home water use in Ireland
cards.comment: Uisce Éireann says the average person here gets through 133 litres a day at home. About a third of it goes down the toilet.
cards.source: Uisce Éireann water conservation guidance, reported by The Irish Times, July 2025; toilet share from water.ie
cards.unit_detail: per person per day, direct domestic use
cards.note: Uisce Éireann also puts the average household at about 125,000 L a year (about 342 L a day). Within 10% of the Europe row (124 L), so the two are never paired.

cards.title: Household water use per person per day (USA)
cards.sub: one day of home water use in the USA
cards.comment: Americans use roughly two and a half times as much water at home as Europeans. That gap is bigger than I expected.
cards.source: US EPA WaterSense / USGS Water Science School
cards.unit_detail: per person per day, direct domestic use (82 US gallons)
cards.excluded_reason: Swapped for the Irish figure (Uisce Éireann, 133 L a day) so home comparisons are local. Kept for reference only.

cards.title: Minimum for basic human needs
cards.sub: one person's basic daily water needs
cards.comment: Fifty litres a day covers drinking, cooking and washing, about one seventh of the average US home use. That's survival, not comfort.
cards.source: WHO, 'How much water is needed in emergencies' (50-100 L/person/day)
cards.unit_detail: per person per day, WHO guidance for drinking, cooking and hygiene

cards.title: Grapes
cards.comment: Grapes need about 608 litres a kilo. Dried into raisins, that jumps to 2,433.
cards.note: Green 425, blue 97, grey 87. The paper's prose says 'grapes 2400 m3/ton', which matches dried grapes (2433), not fresh.

cards.title: Strawberries
cards.comment: Strawberries need just 347 litres a kilo. That is less than half of an apple.
cards.note: Green 201, blue 109, grey 37.

cards.title: Pineapple
cards.comment: Only 9 of a pineapple's 255 litres come from irrigation. Rain does nearly all the work.
cards.note: Green 215, blue 9, grey 31. Pineapple juice is 1273.

cards.title: Mangoes
cards.comment: A kilo of mango needs about 1,800 litres. That is more than twice an apple.
cards.note: FAO group 'Mangoes, mangosteens, guavas'. Green 1314, blue 362, grey 124.

cards.title: Pears
cards.comment: A kilo of pears takes 922 litres. That is about a hundred more than apples.
cards.note: Green 645, blue 94, grey 183. Close to peaches (910).

cards.title: Peaches and nectarines
cards.comment: About a fifth of a peach's 910 litres is irrigation water.
cards.note: Peaches and nectarines combined. Green 583, blue 188, grey 139.

cards.title: Plums
cards.comment: Plums surprised me. At 2,180 litres a kilo, they need over two and a half times an apple.
cards.note: Plums and sloes. Green 1570, blue 188, grey 422.

cards.title: Cherries
cards.comment: A third of the water behind cherries is irrigation, taken from rivers and wells.
cards.note: Sweet cherries. Green 961, blue 531, grey 112. Sour cherries are 1411.

cards.title: Lemons and limes
cards.comment: Lemons need a little more water than oranges, 642 litres a kilo against 560.
cards.note: Lemons and limes combined. Green 432, blue 152, grey 58.

cards.title: Watermelon
cards.comment: Watermelon is full of water, yet it needs just 235 litres a kilo. Lowest fruit in the study.
cards.note: Green 147, blue 25, grey 63. Lowest fruit value in Table 3.

cards.title: Dates
cards.comment: More than half of a date's water is irrigation, 1,250 of its 2,277 litres.
cards.note: Green 930, blue 1250, grey 98.

cards.title: Figs
cards.comment: Figs need 3,350 litres a kilo. That is about four times an apple.
cards.note: Green 1527, blue 1595, grey 228. Fresh figs.

cards.title: Kiwi fruit
cards.comment: Kiwi needs 514 litres a kilo, less than a banana.
cards.note: Green 307, blue 168, grey 38.

cards.title: Raspberries
cards.comment: Raspberries need 413 litres a kilo, only a little more than strawberries.
cards.note: Green 293, blue 53, grey 67.

cards.title: Blueberries
cards.comment: Blueberries need about twice the water of raspberries, 845 litres a kilo.
cards.note: Green 341, blue 334, grey 170. Blue is about 40 percent.

cards.title: Carrots
cards.comment: Carrots need just 195 litres a kilo, the lowest vegetable in the whole study.
cards.note: FAO group 'Carrots and turnips'. Green 106, blue 28, grey 61.

cards.title: Onions (dry)
cards.comment: About a quarter of an onion's water comes from irrigation.
cards.note: Dry bulb onions. Green 192, blue 88, grey 65.

cards.title: Spinach
cards.comment: More than half of spinach's water is grey water, needed to dilute fertiliser runoff.
cards.note: Green 118, blue 14, grey 160. Grey water here relates to nitrogen fertiliser leaching.

cards.title: Broccoli and cauliflower
cards.comment: Broccoli and cauliflower share one figure, 285 litres a kilo. Mostly rain.
cards.note: FAO group 'Cauliflowers and broccoli'. Green 189, blue 21, grey 75.

cards.title: Peas (green)
cards.comment: Fresh peas need 595 litres a kilo. Dried peas need over three times more.
cards.note: Green 382, blue 63, grey 150. Dry peas are 1979.

cards.title: Green beans
cards.comment: A third of the water for green beans is grey water, cleaning up after fertiliser.
cards.note: FAO 'Beans, green'. Green 320, blue 54, grey 188.

cards.title: Garlic
cards.comment: Garlic needs 589 litres a kilo. Ground into garlic powder, it needs 2,265.
cards.note: Green 337, blue 81, grey 170.

cards.title: Pumpkin and squash
cards.comment: Pumpkin needs 336 litres a kilo, about the same as an onion.
cards.note: FAO group 'Pumpkins, squash and gourds'. Green 228, blue 24, grey 84.

cards.title: Peppers (green)
cards.comment: Fresh peppers need 379 litres a kilo. Dried chillies need about 19 times more.
cards.note: FAO 'Chillies and peppers, green'. Green 240, blue 42, grey 97. Dried are 7365.

cards.title: Aubergine
cards.comment: About two thirds of an aubergine's water is rain soaked up from the soil.
cards.note: Green 234, blue 33, grey 95.

cards.title: Asparagus
cards.comment: Asparagus surprised me. At 2,150 litres a kilo, it needs over ten times more than carrots.
cards.note: Green 1524, blue 119, grey 507.

cards.title: Sweet potatoes
cards.comment: Sweet potatoes need a bit more water than ordinary potatoes, 383 litres a kilo against 287.
cards.note: Green 324, blue 5, grey 53.

cards.title: Oats (rolled)
cards.comment: The oat grain needs 1,788 litres a kilo. Rolled into porridge flakes, it becomes 2,416.
cards.note: 'Oats, rolled or flaked grains': green 1998, blue 245, grey 173. Raw oat grain is 1788.

cards.title: Barley
cards.comment: Barley is mostly grown on rain. Only 79 of its 1,423 litres come from irrigation.
cards.note: Green 1213, blue 79, grey 131.

cards.title: Rye
cards.comment: Rye is barely irrigated. Just 25 of its 1,544 litres are irrigation water.
cards.note: Green 1419, blue 25, grey 99. Rye flour is 1930.

cards.title: Millet
cards.comment: Millet needs 4,478 litres a kilo, more than double wheat.
cards.note: Green 4306, blue 57, grey 115. Mostly low-yield rain-fed farming.

cards.title: Sorghum
cards.comment: Almost all of sorghum's 3,048 litres is rain. Irrigation adds only 103.
cards.note: Green 2857, blue 103, grey 87.

cards.title: Chickpeas (dry)
cards.comment: Dried chickpeas need 4,177 litres a kilo, more than twice as much as wheat.
cards.note: Green 2972, blue 224, grey 981.

cards.title: Beans (dry)
cards.comment: Dried beans need 5,053 litres a kilo. Fresh green beans need about a ninth of that.
cards.note: FAO 'Beans, dry' (kidney, haricot). Green 3945, blue 125, grey 983.

cards.title: Peas (dry)
cards.comment: Dried peas need less than half the water of dried beans, 1,979 litres a kilo.
cards.note: Green 1453, blue 33, grey 493.

cards.title: Sunflower oil (refined)
cards.comment: Sunflower oil needs 6,792 litres a kilo, about double the seeds it is pressed from.
cards.note: Green 6088, blue 299, grey 405. Prose rounds to 6800. Seeds are 3366.

cards.title: Rapeseed oil (refined)
cards.comment: Rapeseed oil needs 4,301 litres a kilo, far less than sunflower oil.
cards.note: 'Rape oil, refined'. Green 3226, blue 438, grey 636. Rapeseed itself is 2271.

cards.title: Sesame seeds
cards.comment: Tiny sesame seeds need 9,371 litres a kilo, a touch more than shelled walnuts.
cards.note: Green 8460, blue 509, grey 403. Sesame oil is 21793.

cards.title: Cashew nuts
cards.comment: Cashews need 14,218 litres a kilo. Almost all of it is rain, only 921 litres is irrigation.
cards.note: Green 12853, blue 921, grey 444. FAO code 217, probably in-shell weight, so it may be low for shelled cashews.

cards.title: Pistachios
cards.comment: Two thirds of a pistachio's water is irrigation. No other nut in the study relies on it so much.
cards.note: Green 3095, blue 7602, grey 666. FAO code 223, probably in-shell weight.

cards.title: Hazelnuts (shelled)
cards.comment: Shelled hazelnuts need twice the water of hazelnuts still in their shells.
cards.note: Shelled: green 7627, blue 2180, grey 709. With shell: 5258.

cards.title: Chestnuts
cards.comment: Chestnuts need 2,750 litres a kilo, less than a fifth of cashews.
cards.note: Green 2432, blue 174, grey 144.

cards.title: Coconuts
cards.comment: Nearly all of a coconut's 2,687 litres is rain. Irrigation adds just 2 litres.
cards.note: Green 2669, blue 2, grey 16. Listed under oil crops in the paper.

cards.title: Goat meat
cards.comment: Goat meat needs 5,521 litres a kilo, about half as much as lamb.
cards.source: Mekonnen & Hoekstra 2012, Ecosystems 15:401-415, Table 1 (WFN Report 48, Table 4)
cards.note: Global weighted average. Green 5185, blue 330, grey 6. Grazing 9562, industrial 2863.

cards.title: Milk powder
cards.comment: Take the water out of milk and a kilo of powder takes 4,745 litres to make.
cards.source: Mekonnen & Hoekstra 2012, Ecosystems 15:401-415, Table 1 (WFN Report 48, Table 4)
cards.note: Global weighted average. Green 4011, blue 398, grey 336.

cards.title: Natural rubber
cards.comment: Most of the water behind rubber is rain falling on the trees. About 94 percent is green water.
cards.note: Green 12,964, blue 361, grey 422.

cards.title: Vanilla beans
cards.comment: Vanilla needs more water per kilo than any other crop I found. Over 126,000 litres.
cards.note: Green 86,392, blue 39,048, grey 1,065. Printed as '12 6505' in the table (typesetting space).

cards.title: Bovine leather
cards.comment: A beef cow gives about 6 kg of leather. That leather carries 5.5 percent of the cow's water.
cards.source: WFN Product Gallery, Leather (bovine); Mekonnen & Hoekstra 2010, Report 48
cards.note: 93% green, 4% blue, 3% grey. Report 48 rounds to 17,100; the gallery text rounds to 17,000.

cards.title: Tobacco
cards.comment: A kilo of tobacco leaf needs more than twice the water of a kilo of maize.
cards.note: Green 2,021, blue 205, grey 700. Unmanufactured.

cards.title: Hops
cards.comment: Hops flavour beer. Turn them into hop extract and one kilo needs about 16,000 litres.
cards.note: Hop extract is 16,259 L/kg. Grey water is large for hops (1,414 of 4,065).

cards.title: Cloves
cards.comment: A kilo of cloves needs over 61,000 litres, and nearly all of it is rain.
cards.note: Green 59,834, blue 30, grey 1,341.

cards.title: Cocoa butter
cards.comment: Cocoa butter needs more than twice as much water per kilo as beef.
cards.note: The gallery chocolate text rounds this to 34,000.

cards.title: Jute fibre
cards.comment: Jute needs less than a third of the water cotton lint does.
cards.note: Jute and other bast fibres. Cotton lint is 9,113 L/kg in the same table.

cards.title: Margherita pizza
cards.comment: Half the water in my pizza goes into the mozzarella. The flour takes most of the rest.
cards.source: WFN Product Gallery, Pizza Margherita (Mekonnen & Hoekstra 2011, 2012)
cards.unit_detail: one 725 g pizza margherita, global average
cards.note: Aldaya & Hoekstra 2010 gave 1,216 L for an Italian pizza.

cards.title: Beef burger
cards.comment: A soy burger the same size needs about 158 litres. The beef one needs nearly 15 times more.
cards.source: Ercin, Aldaya & Hoekstra 2011, WFN Report 49 (soy milk and soy burger)
cards.unit_detail: 150 g beef burger, global average
cards.note: Report 16 and Hoekstra 2012 say 2,400 L.

cards.title: Soy burger
cards.comment: Same size as a beef burger, but it needs around 15 times less water.
cards.source: Ercin, Aldaya & Hoekstra 2011, WFN Report 49 (soy milk and soy burger)
cards.unit_detail: 150 g soy burger made in the Netherlands, full supply chain
cards.note: Hoekstra 2012 rounds to about 160 L.

cards.title: Chocolate bar
cards.comment: Cocoa beans need about 20,000 litres a kilo. That is why one bar adds up so fast.
cards.unit_detail: 100 g bar; 40% cocoa paste, 20% cocoa butter, 40% cane sugar
cards.note: Stated in the gallery text. FoE gives 1,430 L for a milk chocolate bar; older Hoekstra slides 2,400 L.

cards.title: Banana
cards.comment: India grows the most bananas. There, a kilo needs less water than the world average.
cards.unit_detail: one large banana, 200 g; 790 L/kg
cards.note: India 500 L/kg.

cards.title: Orange
cards.comment: One orange is about 80 litres. A small glass of orange juice is about 200.
cards.unit_detail: one orange, 150 g; 560 L/kg

cards.title: Glass of orange juice
cards.sub: one glass of orange juice (200 ml)
cards.comment: Orange juice needs about 1,020 litres per litre. One small glass is about 200.
cards.unit_detail: 200 ml glass
cards.note: Report 16 (2004) gave 170 L.

cards.title: Glass of apple juice
cards.sub: one glass of apple juice (200 ml)
cards.comment: One apple is about 125 litres. A glass of apple juice needs almost twice that.
cards.unit_detail: 200 ml glass; apple juice is 1,140 L per litre
cards.note: Report 16 (2004) gave 190 L.

cards.title: Pint of beer
cards.comment: A pint takes about 169 litres, and that only counts the barley.
cards.source: Derived from WFN Product Gallery, Beer (298 L per litre)
cards.note: Barley only: WFN excludes hops and other ingredients.

cards.title: Beef steak
cards.comment: About 99 percent of the water in beef goes into growing the animal's feed.
cards.source: Derived from Mekonnen & Hoekstra 2012 (15,415 L/kg x 0.3 kg); WFN Product Gallery, Beef
cards.unit_detail: 300 g beef, global average
cards.note: The Hoekstra & Chapagain 2008 poster gives 4,650 L for a 300 g steak.

cards.title: Chicken curry ready meal
cards.sub: one 350 g chicken curry ready meal
cards.comment: In this curry, the sauce needed more water than the chicken did.
cards.source: Friends of the Earth / Trucost 2015, Mind your step
cards.unit_detail: 350 g meal: 147 g chicken, 203 g sauce
cards.note: Green 1,817, blue 163, grey 615. Sauce 1,420 L. Trucost model, not WFN.

cards.title: Single cotton bed sheet
cards.sub: one single cotton bed sheet (900 g)
cards.comment: About 42 percent of the water behind cotton goods is blue water, taken from rivers and aquifers.
cards.source: Chapagain, Hoekstra, Savenije & Gautam 2006, Ecological Economics 60:186-203, Table 9
cards.unit_detail: single bed sheet, 900 g, global average
cards.note: Blue 4,400, green 4,000, dilution 1,350.

cards.title: Leather boots
cards.sub: one pair of leather boots, tannery waste treated
cards.comment: When the tannery treats its waste water, a pair of boots needs 42 percent less water.
cards.source: Friends of the Earth / Trucost 2015, Mind your step
cards.unit_detail: one pair of cow-hide boots, tannery effluent treated
cards.note: About 10,700 L is green water for cattle feed.

cards.title: Leather boots, untreated tannery waste
cards.sub: one pair of leather boots, tannery waste untreated
cards.comment: Untreated tannery waste needs so much water to dilute that one pair reaches about 25,000 litres.
cards.source: Friends of the Earth / Trucost 2015, Mind your step
cards.unit_detail: same boots, tannery effluent untreated (grey water about 13,730 L)
cards.note: Stated as about 25,000 L.

cards.title: Microchip
cards.comment: A memory chip weighs just 2 grams, yet making one uses about 32 litres of water.
cards.source: Chapagain & Hoekstra 2004, Water footprints of nations, WFN Report 16, Table 4.2
cards.unit_detail: one 2 g memory chip
cards.note: Industrial process water (via Williams et al. 2002), not a full green/blue/grey supply-chain footprint. Old data.

cards.title: Washing up by hand (12 place settings)
cards.sub: one full load of dishes washed by hand
cards.comment: People in a European study used about 103 litres to wash a full load by hand. Some used over 400.
cards.source: Stamminger et al. 2003, A European Comparison of Cleaning Dishes by Hand, EEDAL, University of Bonn
cards.unit_detail: 12 place settings, average of 113 people from 7 countries; results ran from about 20 L to 447 L
cards.note: Country averages ran from 46 L (Germany) to 170 L (Spain and Portugal). The GB and Ireland row appears to be 63 L, but its label is lost in the extracted text.

cards.title: Power shower (10 minutes)
cards.comment: A long power shower can use nearly twice the water of a bath.
cards.source: Waterwise, How to save water (shower heads use 10 to 15 L a minute)
cards.unit_detail: 10 minutes at 15 L a minute, the top of Waterwise's range
cards.note: Calculated from the flow rate, not measured. Uisce Éireann says shorter showers can save up to 10 L a minute.

cards.title: Washing the car with a hose
cards.sub: one car wash with the hose running
cards.comment: Leave the hose running through a car wash and it can use over 400 litres.
cards.source: RAC Drive, The hosepipe ban: how to keep your car clean (figures credited to Uswitch)
cards.unit_detail: midpoint of 400 to 480 L, hose running the whole time
cards.note: From a comparison site, not a water body. Uisce Éireann says a bucket 'can save hundreds of litres' against a hose, which agrees but gives no number.

cards.title: Washing the car with a bucket
cards.sub: one car wash with a bucket and sponge
cards.comment: Four buckets of about 8 litres will wash a family car.
cards.source: RAC Drive, The hosepipe ban: how to keep your car clean (figures credited to Uswitch)
cards.unit_detail: about four buckets per car

cards.title: Garden sprinkler for an hour
cards.sub: a garden hose or sprinkler running for an hour
cards.comment: Uisce Éireann says an hour of sprinkler uses more than the average family does in a whole day.
cards.source: Uisce Éireann, quoted in the Anglo Celt, 22 July 2026
cards.unit_detail: about 1,000 L an hour

cards.title: Cup of instant coffee
cards.comment: A cup of instant uses only about 2 grams of coffee, so it needs less water than a brewed cup.
cards.unit_detail: 125 ml cup with about 2 g of instant coffee

cards.title: Litre of cow's milk (freshwater withdrawn)
cards.sub: one litre of dairy milk, freshwater taken from rivers and ground
cards.comment: Globally, cow's milk takes about 628 litres of river and ground water per litre.
cards.source: Poore & Nemecek 2018, Science 360:987-992, via Our World in Data
cards.unit_detail: freshwater withdrawn across the supply chain, global average (628.2)
cards.note: Irish dairy is mostly rain-fed grass, so its real withdrawal is probably well below this.
cards.excluded_reason: Measures freshwater withdrawn (Poore & Nemecek 2018), not a full green, blue and grey footprint, so it only appears in its own dilemma, never against other cards.

cards.title: Litre of oat milk (freshwater withdrawn)
cards.sub: one litre of oat milk, freshwater taken from rivers and ground
cards.comment: Oat milk takes about 48 litres of river and ground water per litre. Soy milk is lower still.
cards.source: Poore & Nemecek 2018, Science 360:987-992, via Our World in Data
cards.unit_detail: freshwater withdrawn across the supply chain, global average (48.24)
cards.note: Soy 27.8, rice 269.8, almond 371.5 L per litre in the same data.
cards.excluded_reason: Measures freshwater withdrawn (Poore & Nemecek 2018), not a full green, blue and grey footprint, so it only appears in its own dilemma, never against other cards.

actions.action: Swap one beef meal a week for chicken, or for beans and lentils.
actions.number: A 200 g beef portion is 3,083 L; the same portion of chicken is 865 L.
actions.arithmetic: (15,415 - 4,325) L/kg x 0.2 kg = 2,218 L saved per meal; x 52 weeks = about 115,000 L a year
actions.framing: Biggest single lever in the whole dataset. One meal, not your whole diet.

actions.saving: 5,060 L per wasted kilo of cheese
actions.action: Eat what you buy: finish the cheese, the bread and the leftovers before they go off.
actions.number: A wasted 1 kg block of cheese throws away 5,060 L; a wasted 800 g loaf, 1,286 L.
actions.framing: Food you already own is the cheapest water saving available.

actions.action: Get one more year out of the clothes you own before replacing them.
actions.number: One t-shirt is 2,495 L and one pair of jeans is 8,000 L.
actions.arithmetic: 2,495 + 8,000 = 10,495 L for a single shirt-and-jeans replacement avoided
actions.framing: One garment not bought beats months of shorter showers.

actions.action: Turn the tap off while you brush.
actions.number: 12 L becomes 1 L, twice a day.
actions.framing: Costs nothing, and it is about three t-shirts' worth of water a year.

actions.number: Uisce Éireann says fixing a dripping tap saves about 150 L a week, about 21 L a day.
actions.arithmetic: 21 L/day x 365 = 7,665 L a year, roughly 96 baths
actions.framing: A ten-minute job that runs in the background for the rest of the year.

actions.action: Take two minutes off your shower.
actions.number: Uisce Éireann says the average shower runs at 7 L a minute.
actions.arithmetic: 7 L/min x 2 min x 365 = 5,110 L a year
actions.framing: Same order of magnitude as the toothbrush habit. Small, but it compounds daily.

comparisons.line: One beef burger (150 g patty) = about 47 showers.
One cup of coffee = 11 tooth-brushings with the tap left running.
comparisons.arithmetic: 132 L per cup / 12 L per 2-min running-tap brushing = 11.0
relates_to: Brushing teeth with the tap running

comparisons.line: One cotton t-shirt = 51 showers, or 19 days of one person's home water use in Ireland.
comparisons.arithmetic: 2,495 L / 49 L = 50.9 showers; 2,495 / 133 L per person per day = 18.8 days
relates_to: Household water use per person per day (Ireland)

comparisons.line: One pair of jeans = 60 days of everything one person in Ireland does with water at home.
comparisons.arithmetic: 8,000 L / 133 L per person per day = 60.2 days
relates_to: Household water use per person per day (Ireland)

comparisons.line: One egg = 33 flushes of a modern dual-flush toilet.
One kilo of cheese = 78 washing-machine cycles.
One kilo of beef = 116 days of one person's home water use in Ireland.
comparisons.arithmetic: 15,415 L / 133 L per person per day = 115.9 days
relates_to: Household water use per person per day (Ireland)

comparisons.line: A small glass of wine = more water than a full bath.
comparisons.arithmetic: 109 L per 125 ml glass vs 80 L per bath = 1.36x

comparisons.line: A whole kilo of lettuce = 3 baths. A kilo of lamb = 130 baths.
Swapping one coffee for one tea saves as much water as skipping a bath and a third.
comparisons.arithmetic: 132 L - 27 L = 105 L saved; 105 / 80 L per bath = 1.31

dilemmas.guess: Washing up by hand (12 place settings)
dilemmas.basis: for one full load of dishes
dilemmas.comment: I assumed the sink would win. It does not. People in the study used about 103 litres by hand, and a full dishwasher uses about 20.
dilemmas.caveat: A careful washer with a basin can beat the machine, and a half-empty dishwasher changes the maths.

dilemmas.comment: The shower wins. Seven minutes is about 49 litres, a bath about 80.
dilemmas.caveat: A long or power shower can pass a bath, so it comes down to the minutes.

dilemmas.comment: This one surprised me. Ten minutes under a power shower can use nearly twice a bath.
dilemmas.caveat: That is a flow rate times minutes, not a measurement. An electric shower runs much slower.

dilemmas.known: Brushing teeth with the tap off
dilemmas.guess: Brushing teeth with the tap running
dilemmas.comment: Leaving the tap on uses about twelve times more. One litre does the job just fine.
dilemmas.caveat: Tap flow varies, and a trickle uses far less than 6 litres a minute.

dilemmas.comment: An old cistern can use more than twice a modern full flush. Uisce Éireann says a third of home water goes down the toilet.
dilemmas.caveat: Many old cisterns hold 9 litres, not 13. A leaking valve can waste more than either.

dilemmas.known: Washing the car with a bucket
dilemmas.guess: Washing the car with a hose
dilemmas.comment: Uisce Éireann says a bucket can save hundreds of litres. The estimate I found was about 440 by hose and 32 by bucket.
dilemmas.caveat: That assumes the hose runs the whole time. A trigger nozzle closes the gap a lot.

dilemmas.basis: for one cup, counting the water to grow and make it
dilemmas.comment: Good news for tea drinkers. A cup of coffee takes about 132 litres, a cup of tea about 27.
dilemmas.caveat: This is hidden water, mostly rain on farms, not tap water. Milk adds to both.

dilemmas.basis: for one cup of coffee, counting the water to grow and make it
dilemmas.comment: I guessed instant would be worse because of the factory. It is not. A cup uses less coffee, so about 80 litres against 132.
dilemmas.caveat: A strong brewed cup uses more coffee and a weak one less, so the gap moves.

dilemmas.comment: Same size, very different water. The beef burger needs about 15 times more, mostly rain on grass and feed crops.
dilemmas.caveat: Irish grass-fed beef uses little irrigation, so the gap in tap-type water is smaller. Beef still uses more.

dilemmas.basis: per litre, counting only water taken from rivers and the ground
dilemmas.comment: Cow's milk takes about thirteen times the river and ground water of oat milk. Almond milk sits in between, which I did not expect.
dilemmas.caveat: That is a global average. Irish dairy is mostly rain-fed grass, so it takes far less than this. Oat milk still comes out lower.
